what_it_does: Every processor needs a 'decoder' — a circuit that reads the binary code of an instruction (like 'add these two numbers') and figures out exactly what the processor should do. Writing this decoder by hand for a complex instruction set (the full vocabulary a processor understands) is tedious and error-prone, especially when the instruction encoding is irregular: different instructions use different bit patterns, conditions, and special cases. This paper automates decoder generation by borrowing a technique from machine learning — decision trees — and adapting it using information theory (a mathematical framework for measuring how much a question reduces uncertainty) to pick the most informative bit to test at each branch. The result is a decoder that is both correct and compact, generated automatically from a formal description of the instruction set.
